settings.description: In May 2024, over 65,000 developers responded to our annual survey about coding, the technologies and tools they use and want to learn, AI, and developer experience at work. Check out the results and see what's new for Stack Overflow users.

chapters.name: Overview
chapters.description:
Welcome to the 2024 Developer Survey! For 14 years, we've delivered industry-leading insights into the developer community. 

This is the voice of the developer. Analysts, IT leaders, reporters, and other developers turn to this report to stay up-to-date with the evolving developer experience, see which technologies are rising or falling in favor, and understand where tech might be going next.
  
Happy reading!

chapters.name: Developer Profile
chapters.description: What we know about the global community of developers.

questions.name: Educational attainment
questions.description: 66% of developers have a BA/BS or MA/MS degree despite only 49% of developers learning to code at school.

questions.name: Learning to code
questions.description:
Online resources are the top choice for developers to learn code according to 82% of responses. 

Respondents 18 - 24 years old are most likely to learn code at traditional schools of all the age groups, and consistently so for the last three years.

questions.name: Online resources to learn how to code
questions.description: Technical documentation (84%) and Stack Overflow (80%) continue to be the top online resources to learn code. 37% of responses indicate AI is helping them learn, too.

questions.name: Technical documentation preferences to learn how to code
questions.description: API and SDK documents are the documentation source of choice for 90% of developers.

questions.name: Years coding
questions.description: More than 1 in 3 developers that took the survey this year have been coding as long as or longer than Stack Overflow existed. 38% of respondents have been coding for 15 years or more.

questions.name: Years coding professionally
questions.description: 1 in 3 developers have been coding professionally for four years or less.

questions.name: Years of professional coding experience by developer type
questions.description: People managers such as executives and engineering managers are reporting the highest average years of coding this year with more than 15 years of experience, while popular developer roles such as back-end and full-stack developers are reporting 10-11 years experience on average.

questions.name: Developer type
questions.description:
Full-stack, back-end, and front-end developers were the top three roles reported by developers for the last three years; however, front-end developers have decreased from 6.6% to 5.6% since last year. 
This year, more developers identify as students than as front-end employees and we saw a slight increase in developers who have an embedded applications role or are academic researchers.

questions.name: Geography
questions.description: 52% of respondents shared their country in this year's survey. The top 10 countries account for 60% of those that were given, and Europe accounts for most of the top-responding countries.

questions.name: Age
questions.description: Most developers in the survey this year report being 25 - 34 years old (37%). That number increases for professional developers to 42% and has steadily decreased in the last three years for those learning to code from 17% in 2022 to 12% this year.

chapters.name: Technology
chapters.description:
Each year we explore the tools and technologies developers are currently using and the ones they want to use. 

This year, we included new questions about embedded technology tools and industry-sourced, community-vetted technology options.

questions.name: Programming, scripting, and markup languages
questions.description: JavaScript has been a mainstay in the developer survey and on Stack Overflow since our first survey. The most popular programming language has been JavaScript every year we have done the survey except for 2013 and 2014, when SQL was the most popular language.

questions.name: Databases
questions.description: PostgreSQL debuted in the developer survey in 2018 when 33% of developers reported using it, compared with the most popular option that year: MySQL, in use by 59% of developers. Six years later, PostgreSQL is used by 49% of developers and is the most popular database for the second year in a row.

questions.name: Cloud platforms
questions.description: AWS' share of usage amongst respondents is the same in 2024 as in 2023, while Azure and Google Cloud increased their share. Azure has climbed from 26% to 28% usage and Google Cloud went from 24% to 25%.

questions.name: Web frameworks and technologies
questions.description: Node.js peaked in 2020 with its highest recorded usage score of 51%. While not as popular, it's still the most used web technology in the survey this year and has increased popularity among those learning to code from last year.

questions.name: Embedded Technologies
questions.description: Embedded technologies is a new sub-section of the developer survey this year. 30% of developers are using Raspberry Pi, making it the first most popular embedded technology in the Developer Survey.

questions.name: Other frameworks and libraries
questions.description: .NET is the most used among other frameworks and libraries again this year for all developers. Those learning to code are using NumPy and Pandas the most (as they were last year).

questions.name: Other tools
questions.description: Docker is used the most by professional developers (59%) and npm is used the most by developers learning to code (45%).

questions.name: Integrated development environment
questions.description: Visual Studio Code is used by more than twice as many developers than its nearest (and related) alternative, Visual Studio.

questions.name: Asynchronous tools
questions.description: Jira and Confluence top the list for most used asynchronous tools developers use for the third year.

questions.name: Synchronous tools
questions.description: Teams is the most popular synchronous tool for professional developers (and overall) while Discord is the most popular amongst those learning to code.

questions.name: Operating system
questions.description: Windows is the most popular operating system for developers, across both personal and professional use.

questions.name: AI Search and Developer Tools
questions.description: ChatGPT is used by twice as many developers as its next closest alternative, GitHub Copilot. ChatGPT has a popular free option that developers observably like.

questions.name: Programming, scripting, and markup languages
questions.description: JavaScript, Python and SQL are all highly-desired and admired programming languages, but Rust continues to be the most-admired programming language with an 83% score this year.

questions.name: Databases
questions.description: SQLite increased its desired score this year to become wanted by more developers than MySQL compared to last year, increasing from 23% to 27%. If you're curious about SQLite, listen to our podcast interview with the creator.

questions.name: Cloud platforms
questions.description: Hetzner is the most-admired cloud platform for the second year in a row with a 75% admire score, rising from their 70% score last year.

questions.name: Web frameworks and technologies
questions.description: 73% of developers that used it want to keep working with Svelte. Fun fact: Our team at Stack Overflow used Svelte for the first time in building our 2024 Developer Survey results site. We could go on and on about Svelte, listen to us do just that in a interview with one of our own.

questions.name: Embedded Technologies
questions.description: New to the survey this year, Cargo comes in with a very weighty 83% admire score.

questions.name: Other frameworks and libraries
questions.description: Ruff is a new addition to technologies listed in the survey this year, and developers love it: 84% of those that use Ruff want to continue using it.

questions.name: Other tools
questions.description: Docker users have elevated this tool to most-admired (78%) this year along with being most-desired for the second year in a row.

questions.name: Integrated development environment
questions.description: Visual Studio Code is the most-desired (and used) IDE tool (59%) for developers but the most-admired is Neovim (83%).

questions.name: Asynchronous tools
questions.description: Markdown wins the popularity contest with developers this year! Not only do users say they admire it more this year than last (84% vs. 82%), but Markdown also received the highest admired score of all technologies on our survey this year.

questions.name: Synchronous tools
questions.description: Signal users greatly admire the tool (74% admiration score) despite its being ranked eighth on the list for synchronous tools users want to use.

questions.name: AI Search and Developer Tools
questions.description: Most developers who use ChatGPT want to keep using it (75% Admired), while most who use Replit Ghostwrite or Tabnine are least likely to keep using it (36% Admired). If you aren't familiar with Replit, we have an interview for you to familiarize yourself.

sections.name: Worked with vs. want to work with

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Programming, scripting, and markup languages
questions.description: Those learning to code want to try more languages next year compared to their professional counterparts. On average, each user who is learning to code wants to try 12 other languages in the next year versus users who are professional devs who want to try eight.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Databases
questions.description: 28% of PostgreSQL users would like to use Redis next year.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Cloud platforms
questions.description: 22% of Microsoft Azure users and 24% of AWS users would like to use Google Cloud next year. Google Cloud users would like to use tools that are lesser known next year, such as Supabase, Vercel, and Cloudflare.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Web frameworks and technologies
questions.description: The top web framework Node.js users want to use next year is React (45%), while not many React users want to use Node.js, but would like to use Next.js (34%). Meanwhile, most Next.js users indicated the only tool they want to work with next year is Next.js.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Embedded Technologies
questions.description: 53% of users who used Arduino this year want to use Raspberry Pi next, but no Raspberry Pi users want to use Arduino next.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Other frameworks and libraries
questions.description: Developers who used Numpy or Pandas in the last year are interested in trying the most other frameworks or libraries next year: Numpy users are interested in trying 24 and Pandas users are interested in 22 next year.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Other tools
questions.description: Docker users, of which there are many, are interested in trying Kubernetes, Vite, Terraform, and Ansible next year.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Integrated development environment
questions.description: 74% of respondents used Visual Studio Code this past year, and of those that may want to try a different IDE next year are only interested in Vim or Neovim. Vim and Neovim users are mostly interested in staying put.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Asynchronous tools
questions.description: Now that's brand loyalty: Obsidian users have no desire to try any other asynchronous tools next year, and nine different groups of asynchronous tools users would like to switch to see why next year.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: Synchronous tools
questions.description: 27% of Microsoft Teams users would like to use Slack next year, but the feeling is not mutual: less than 2% of Slack users reported wanting to use Microsoft Teams next year.

questions.section: Worked with vs. want to work with
questions.name: AI Search and Developer Tools
questions.description: Most developers use ChatGPT of all the AI tools, and 74% want to keep using it next year. 41% of ChatGPT users want to use GitHub Copilot next year.

questions.name: Top paying technologies
questions.description: Erlang developers take the top spot this year for highest reported median salary.

questions.name: Change in salaries between 2023 and 2024
questions.description: Nim, Erlang, and Apex developers all saw an increase in the median reported salary in 2024. All other developer technologies reported a decrease in median salary.

chapters.name: AI
chapters.description: In this section we gain insight into the real sentiments behind the surge in AI popularity. Is it making a real impact in the way developers work or is it all hype?

questions.name: AI tools in the development process
questions.description: 76% of all respondents are using or are planning to use AI tools in their development process this year, an increase from last year (70%). Many more developers are currently using AI tools this year, too (62% vs. 44%).

questions.name: AI tool sentiment
questions.description: 72% of all respondents are favorable or very favorable of AI tools for development. This is lower than last year's favorability of 77%; a decline in favorability could be due to disappointing results from usage.

questions.name: Benefits of AI tools
questions.description: 81% agree increasing productivity is the biggest benefit that developers identify for AI tools. Speeding up learning is seen as a bigger benefit to developers learning to code (71%) compared to professional developers (61%).

questions.name: Accuracy of AI tools
questions.description: Similar to last year, developers remain split on whether they trust AI output: 43% feel good about AI accuracy and 31% are skeptical. Developers learning to code are trusting AI accuracy more than their professional counterparts (49% vs. 42%).

questions.name: AI tools' ability to handle complex tasks
questions.description: The development workflow is complicated, as the abundance of questions and answers on Stack Overflow can attest to. Almost half (45%) of professional developers believe AI tools are bad or very bad at handling complex tasks.

questions.name: AI in the development workflow
questions.description: Developers currently using AI tools mostly use them to write code (82%) and those who are interested but not yet using AI tools are mostly curious about testing code (46%). Developers with experience can trust AI tools to help write code to get started but perhaps know testing is a complex step best left to traditional processes.

questions.name: AI tools next year
questions.description: In the next year, most developers agree that AI tools will be more integrated mostly in the ways they are documenting code (81%), testing code (80%), and writing code (76%).

questions.name: Are AI tools a threat to your job
questions.description: 70% of professional developers do not perceive AI as a threat to their job.

questions.name: Most important ethical issues for AI
questions.description: Misinformation and disinformation in AI results are a top ethical concern in this year's survey for 79% of developers. Source attribution is the next top ethical concern (65%) which Stack Overflow is working to protect for our community members.

questions.name: Challenges with AI at work
questions.description: Professional developers agree the issue is not user error: twice as many professionals cite lack of trust or understanding the codebase as the top challenge of AI tools compared to proper training.

questions.name: AI at work in one year
questions.description:
Developers most frequently hypothesize the amount of time they spend on tasks with AI tools and the complexity of those tasks will be different one year from now.

By grouping open-ended responses into topics based on phrase patterns, we can see themes amongst developer responses.

chapters.name: Work
chapters.description: Developers tell us about workplace trends and offer some transparency about salary for different roles and experience levels.

questions.name: Employment status
questions.description: 84% of respondents are working: either part-time, freelancing, or full-time.

questions.name: Employment status by geography
questions.description: Full-time employment has decreased in the U.S. since last year's survey (69% to 65%). Looking at employment in the top five countries, in the U.K. and Ukraine respondents not employed full-time are more likely to be independent contractors and in Germany and India are more likely to be a full-time student if not employed full-time.

questions.name: Work environment
questions.description: The number of hybrid developers has stayed consistent this year with last year (42%), while the percentage of developers working in-person has increased (20%) for the third year in a row compared to 15% in 2022 and 16% in 2023.

questions.name: Company size
questions.description: 47% of respondents work for organizations that have fewer than 100 employees.

questions.name: Salary by developer type
questions.description:
The highest-paid developers of all respondents are site reliability and cloud infrastructure engineers, as both roles are pivotal in keeping digital services up and running. 

Looking at top-responding regions, mobile developers report higher earnings in the U.S., data engineers are the highest-paid in Germany and Ukraine, and back-end developers are top earners in India and the U.K.

questions.name: Salary and experience by developer type
questions.description: Developer experience is highly valued and this is confirmed by this year's top-earning roles that relate to the DevRel scaffolding. Senior executives are making the most with the most experience on average, followed by developer advocates, engineering managers, and developer experience professionals.

questions.name: Salary and experience by language
questions.description:
Developers that are using Erlang and Clojure are top earners in the past year, averaging more than $95K annually (USD) with about 12 years experience. Developers working with Dart and Prolog are earning the least annually (< $45K annual USD) with less experience on average (< 10 years). 

Most developers are reporting their salary range is averaging $10K USD less this year: $60 - $75K USD compared to $70 - $85K USD in 2023.

questions.name: Influence on technology purchases
questions.description: Most respondents have influence over technology purchases (62%). Those roles with the highest levels of influence are senior executives (99%), engineering managers (87%), and product managers (77%).

questions.name: Prefer to build and/or buy new tech
questions.description: 60% of respondents endorse technology purchases that are build-and-buy as opposed to purely build or buy. Database administrators, developer advocates, and security professionals are less likely to endorse a build-and-buy approach possibly due to the need to document and safeguard customizations.

questions.name: Researching new tools and technologies
questions.description:
Starting a free trial is the most common way to evaluate new tools (75%) followed closely by asking other developers (73%).

Backend developers, embedded app developers, and academic researchers prefer to ask other developers than to start a free trial.

questions.name: Tech endorsement factors
questions.description: APIs are pretty cool, but did you know that 75% of developers are more likely to endorse your technology if you provide access to APIs? Make sure to let back-end developers and engineering managers know about the API integrations you offer: they are even more likely to endorse your tech than the average coder.

questions.name: Coding outside of work
questions.description: Most developers code outside of work as a hobby (68%), and almost 40% code outside of work for professional development or self-paced learning from online courses.

chapters.name: Community
chapters.description: Community is at the center of all that we do. Here we take a look at how people use Stack Overflow and how connected they feel to the community.

questions.name: Visiting sites across Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange
questions.description: Most everyone has visited Stack Overflow, but many fewer visited the Stack Overflow blog and podcast (15% overall). You are in for a content treat, make sure to visit our blog site to see new articles and interviews posted every week!

questions.name: Frequency of visiting Stack Overflow
questions.description: 93% of respondents visit Stack Overflow at least multiple times per month if not multiple times per day.

questions.name: Have an account on Stack Overflow
questions.description: We love to see it: 76% of respondents say they have an account on Stack Overflow!

questions.name: Frequency of participation on Stack Overflow
questions.description: Those learning to code are almost twice as likely to have not participated in Q&A on Stack Overflow than professional developers. We know the first step can sometimes be the hardest: that's why we recently launched a better experience for newbies. Get those questions ready and check out Staging Ground .

questions.name: How you choose to use Stack Overflow
questions.description: Everyone agrees that finding answers quickly is the primary reason to use Stack Overflow. Understandably, those learning to code are more likely to use Stack Overflow to learn coding skills than professional developers or other coders.

questions.name: Feel like a part of the Stack Overflow community
questions.description: 34% of respondents feel like they are a member of the Stack Overflow community. Respondents between ages 45 - 64 are the most likely to feel included (> 40%).

questions.name: Top suggested improvements per frequency of participation
questions.description:
We asked and you answered: many suggested improvements indicate a desire for fresh perspectives on Stack Overflow. 

By grouping open-ended responses into topics based on phrase patterns, we can see themes amongst different users.

chapters.name: Professional Developers
chapters.description: We asked Professional Developers to tell us about what impacts their productivity at work, how often it happens, and how much time it takes out of their day. We also asked them about the developer experience at work—do they have the processes, tools, and programs they need to make their jobs easier?

questions.name: Participation in Professional Developer series
questions.description: Roughly 29K professional developers contributed to this year's Professional Developer section of questions from the Developer Survey all about productivity and satisfaction at work.

questions.name: Individual contributor or people manager
questions.description: Coders are coding more than managing: 87% of professional developers indicate they are in individual contributor roles.

questions.name: Years of professional work experience
questions.description: 1 in 4 are 1 to 4: as in 25% of professional developers report having one to four years of work experience. The majority of respondents are early-to-mid career professionals (nine or less years experience) and the majority of people managers are mid-to-later career professionals (10+ years experience).

questions.name: Ability to find knowledge and information within their organization
questions.description:
70% of respondents agree or strongly agree that they know where to go to find answers to their questions and 56% agree they can do so quickly. 

How quick is quickly? 53% agree or strongly agree that waiting on answers disrupts their workflow, even if they know where to go to find those answers.

questions.name: Frequency of productivity frictions
questions.description:
30% of developers say knowledge silos impact their productivity ten or more times per week. 

Knowledge silos aren't a problem for everyone (45% agree or strongly agree that they are a nuisance), but if you have them, they are a frequent problem.

questions.name: Daily time spent searching for answers/solutions
questions.description:
61% of all respondents spend more than 30 minutes a day searching for answers or solutions to problems. 

People managers spend less time searching than individual contributors (40% vs. 36% spend 30 minutes or less).

questions.name: Daily time spent answering questions
questions.description: People managers spend a lot of time answering questions: 61% spend more than 30 minutes a day answering questions.

questions.name: Processes, tools, and programs within an organization
questions.description:
Most professional developers report having CI/CD, DevOps, and automated testing available at their organization. 

The percentage of developers with access to AI-assisted technology at work doubled: 15.7% last year to 32.4% this year.

questions.name: Cloud on On-prem environments
questions.description: Most developers work in cloud-hosted or hybrid environments (86%); 14% work with solely on-prem environments.

questions.name: Resources for technical questions at work
questions.description: Public search engines are the top resource used by professional developers to find answers to technical questions. 55% use traditional search and 15% use AI-powered search, either free or paid.

questions.name: Most common frustrations
questions.description:
Technical debt is the top frustration at work for professional developers according to 63% of respondents, regardless of whether they are an individual contributor or a people manager. 

However, they don't agree on how frustrating unreliable tools and services at work can be: people managers agree this is second to tech debt, but individual contributors find complex tech stacks for building or deployment to be slightly more frustrating.

questions.name: Industry
questions.description: Software development remains a top industry for developers. 41% of respondents who participated in the professional developer section of this year's survey are working in the software development industry.

questions.name: Satisfied at current job
questions.description: Only one in five professional developers are happy with their current job. We asked whether they were satisfied with their current role, and 48% indicated they were complacent while 19% were satisfied.

questions.name: Factors that most contribute to job satisfaction
questions.description: Happy, unhappy, or somewhere in between, all professional developers agree that improving quality of code and developer environments provide the most satisfaction at work.
65,437 responses from 185 countries are used in these survey results.

An attention check question, a consent question and the question asking "Which of the following options best describes you today?" were all used as qualifiers in the responses we kept for analysis.  ~20K responses were not used.
48,019 responses were used to provide aggregated salary information.
The survey was fielded from May 19, 2024 to June 20, 2024.
The median time spent on the survey for qualified responses was almost 21 minutes, an increase we expected this year because of additional questions asked.

Respondents were recruited primarily through channels owned by Stack Overflow. The top sources of respondents were onsite messaging, blog posts, email/newsletter subscribers, banner ads, and social media posts. Since respondents were recruited in this way, highly-engaged users on Stack Overflow were more likely to notice the prompts to take the survey over the duration of the collection promotion.
We converted salaries from user currencies to USD using the exchange rate on June 11, 2024.
Some questions that are multi-select for the available choices have switched to be displayed as a percentage of total unique responses instead of total frequency of responses this year.

questions.name: How do you feel about the length of the survey this year?
How easy or difficult was this survey to complete?
